# Akbr Kanyesigye

> Akbr Kanyesigye, software and data engineer in Kampala. Census systems, data pipelines, dashboards, and AI that answers from Uganda's official statistics.

This is the full plain-text version of https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/, generated from the site on 2026-09-24. A shorter index lives at https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/llms.txt.

## About

I build the systems that move public data from collection to use.

Software and data engineer in Kampala. I work along the whole path a figure takes: the tools that collect it, the pipelines that process it, the dashboards that show it, and the AI that answers from it.

## Now

- **A prediction market for Africa**, in the spirit of Polymarket: markets on the questions people here actually argue about, settled on sources they can check.
- **Sanyu**, the Bureau's AI assistant over official statistics: more datasets, drafted statistical briefs, and a short code of practice for AI over official figures.
- **A harmonised data portal** that brings datasets from across government agencies into one place, so service delivery can rest on shared figures.
- **Open tools for census and survey teams**: csync, which syncs CSPro data with your own code, and a CSPro skill that teaches AI assistants to work on survey apps.
- **TuuraHub**, a property management product for East African landlords, in beta on the side.
- **Azure Data Fundamentals**, the next certificate after AWS Cloud Practitioner.

## Work

Grouped by who the work serves.

### Official statistics, at the Uganda Bureau of Statistics

#### [Sanyu](https://statistics.ubos.org/sanyu) (2024 to now, AI)

Uganda's AI assistant for official statistics.

Ask a question in plain language, in English or one of five Ugandan languages, and get the figure with its source, a live table or chart, or a drafted statistical brief. The language model decides what to retrieve; the statistical database decides what the value is. No figure reaches the reader unless a structured query returned it, and every figure carries its table, survey, period and geography.

- 5,100+: indicators from six official sources
- 1,600+: tables lifted from published reports, citeable by page
- 40 ms: cold start, down from 30 to 60 seconds
- 45: golden-fact regression tests on every build

Built with Node.js, SQLite, LLM tool calling, RAG, MCP endpoints, Python pipelines, Nginx and pm2. Built in-house at UBOS with Sunbird AI on the language side.

Links: [statistics.ubos.org/sanyu](https://statistics.ubos.org/sanyu)

Screenshot: Sanyu's chat screen: a sidebar of data sources such as Census 2024 and CPI, and the prompt 'Ask Sanyu about Uganda's official statistics' (https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/images/shot-sanyu.jpg)

#### Census e-recruitment and field staff management (2023 to 2024, web platform)

The system behind the people who counted Uganda in 2024.

Applications, vetting, shortlists, interviews, assignment and payroll records for the National Population and Housing Census, decentralised to every district, with national dashboards for the Bureau. I was the primary developer and ran its deployment.

- 200,000+: census personnel managed nationwide
- 80%: faster issue resolution from the testing and monitoring tooling around it

Built with Next.js, MongoDB, Docker, AWS.

Screenshot: The national recruitment dashboard, showing applicant totals and a table of applicants per district (https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/images/census-recruitment.jpg)

#### [UBOS dissemination portal](https://statistics.ubos.org/) (2024 to now, data platform)

One home for Uganda's official statistics, across more than six national datasets.

The 2024 National Population and Housing Census down to parish level, the Baseline Education Census 2025 and the Uganda Aquaculture Census 2025 are live, with harmonised community and GBV data, the national standard indicators, the Malaria Indicator Survey 2024-25 and a census-based multidimensional poverty index on the way. Each comes as dashboards, maps and tabulations.

I led a team of three on the platform and built the ingestion and reporting pipelines underneath it, including the PDF table extraction that makes decades of survey reports queryable.

- 6+: national datasets in one place
- 500,000+: public users
- 3: people on the team I led

Built with Python and SQL pipelines, Power BI, QGIS.

Links: [Visit statistics.ubos.org](https://statistics.ubos.org/)

Screenshot: The UBOS dissemination portal: the Census 2024, Baseline Education Census and Aquaculture Census cards, with four more datasets marked coming soon (https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/images/shot-portal.jpg)

#### Also at the Bureau (2023 to now, data work)

Classification, collection tools, GIS tooling, cloud and security.

Automated classification for coding census and survey responses, which removed months of manual work. The data collection instruments used for national enumeration. Python and QGIS tooling that sped up map preparation for the GIS team. The Bureau's AWS and GCP estate, including a shared outbound proxy that consolidated external service access and traffic filtering. Phishing exercises with the security team.

### Tools for census and survey teams

#### [csync, a CSPro synchronisation suite](https://github.com/kanyeceejayA/csync) (2026, open source)

Sync any CSPro survey between a CSWeb server and your own code.

Most census and survey fieldwork in the region runs on CSPro: tablets collect cases and sync them through a CSWeb server. Getting those cases in and out from your own code is the hard part. csync reads a survey's dictionary and does the rest. Pull cases into a plain SQLite store, add, edit or remove them as ordinary Python dictionaries, and push them back so they reach the tablets, with the vector clocks CSEntry expects.

It works for any dictionary, from assignments and staff lists to a full household questionnaire, and speaks both CSWeb 8.0 and 8.1. It comes as a Python library, a command line, a one-page web front end, and readers and writers for CSPro's own data files.

- Any: CSPro dictionary, with no field names hard-coded
- 8.0 and 8.1: CSWeb versions it speaks
- 0: third-party packages the core library needs

Built with Python's standard library, SQLite and the CSWeb REST API, with an optional Flask page.

Links: [csync on GitHub](https://github.com/kanyeceejayA/csync)

#### [CSPro toolkit, a skill for AI assistants](https://github.com/kanyeceejayA/csync/tree/main/skills/cspro-toolkit) (2026, AI)

Teaches Claude and other AI assistants to read, edit and check CSPro survey apps.

A CSPro application is a set of files that must stay in step: the dictionary, the logic, the forms and the run files. CSPro can't compile an entry app from the command line, so an AI assistant editing one is working blind. This skill gives it the map.

It explains what each file is for and how a change in the dictionary ripples into the logic and run files. It adds a linter that pre-checks logic edits before anyone opens CSPro, walks through building and releasing a deployment package, and shows how to ask a CSWeb server for its dictionaries, case counts, sync history and cases. It is packaged as an Agent Skill, the SKILL.md format that Claude and other assistants can load.

Built with Markdown instructions, Python helper scripts, and a reference for the CSWeb API.

Links: [The skill on GitHub](https://github.com/kanyeceejayA/csync/tree/main/skills/cspro-toolkit)

### Civic platforms

#### National Youth Council accountability platform (2024, web platform)

Where Uganda's youth council shows its money.

A public accountability platform for the National Youth Council of Uganda: every project with its location, timeline, budget, funding sources and expenditure updates, downloadable reports, and a way for young people to leave feedback on what was done. Built in 2024 with the support of Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung.

#### Uchaguzi (2021, mobile app, chatbot and site)

Voter information for Uganda's 2021 general elections.

A website, a WhatsApp chatbot and Android and iOS apps that explained how to register, where to vote and what the rules were, for the Ministry of ICT's Government Citizen Interaction Centre and the Electoral Commission, with Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung. I led the team.

- 10,000+: people served during the election

Built with Flutter, Drupal, PHP, Python.

Links: [Read about it on PC Tech](https://pctechmag.com/2021/01/uchaguzi-a-voter-information-platform/)

Screenshot: Uchaguzi app screens on phones (https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/images/uchaguzi.jpg)

#### Youth Action Handbook (2022, mobile app)

A bilingual learning app for young peacebuilders in the Great Lakes.

Courses, quizzes, certificates and a forum for the Great Lakes Youth Network for Dialogue and Peace, an EU and Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung project, on Android, iOS and web in DR Congo, Rwanda and Uganda. I led development from the first screen to the store listings.

Built with Flutter, with offline caching for patchy networks.

Links: [Android](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=ug.rtl.youth_action_handbook), [iOS, archived listing](https://web.archive.org/web/20220626001000/https://apps.apple.com/ug/app/youth-action-handbook/id1614617118)

Screenshot: Four Youth Action Handbook app screens: home, sign in, a course, and a quiz (https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/images/youth-action-handbook.jpg)

#### [Makerere at 100](https://100.mak.ac.ug/) (2022, web platform)

The central platform for Makerere University's centennial.

Donations, merchandise and communications for the celebrations, serving more than 12,000 people. I was the technical lead.

Built with PHP and a custom WordPress theme.

Links: [100.mak.ac.ug](https://100.mak.ac.ug/)

#### BudgetMate (2023, mobile app)

Budget collection for Yemen's Ministry of Finance, with or without internet.

Spending units create budget requests with guided inputs or CSV files in a cross-platform app; where there's no connectivity, the backend exchanges data over an SMS gateway, with each request encrypted. It shared first place at the Yemen Public Financial Management Hackathon, run by the Ministry of Finance with the IMF in Amman in March 2023.

- 1st: place, shared, with a USD 5,000 grant

Built with Expo and React Native, MongoDB, Twilio.

Links: [The hackathon results, archived](https://web.archive.org/web/20230324201431/https://yemenpfmhackathon.com/)

### Products and open source

#### [TuuraHub](https://tuurahub.com) (2026, product in beta)

Property management built for East Africa.

A self-serve platform for landlords and property managers: properties, units, tenants, leases, invoices, receipts, rent reminders by SMS, WhatsApp and email, maintenance tickets, a tenant portal and listings. Built for the large middle between spreadsheets and enterprise suites, with Uganda as the first market. A side product, in beta.

Built with Next.js, Prisma and Postgres, Stripe, AWS S3.

Links: [tuurahub.com](https://tuurahub.com)

Screenshot: The TuuraHub landing page: 'Manage every rental, without the chase' above buttons to create a hub and cards for landlords, renters and tenants (https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/images/shot-tuurahub.jpg)

#### [flutter_fido2](https://github.com/kanyeceejayA/flutter_fido2) (2022, open source)

Sign in without passwords, in Flutter.

An open-source plugin for FIDO2 and WebAuthn: register authenticators, sign challenges and talk to your server, on Android, iOS and Windows, with web support in progress. Built during my master's, with a companion server.

Links: [On GitHub](https://github.com/kanyeceejayA/flutter_fido2)

## Stories behind some of these

### The 4th Industrial Revolution Taskforce

April 2019 to January 2021

In April 2019 President Museveni set up a 21-member expert taskforce, chaired by former ICT minister John Nasasira, to study the technologies of the fourth industrial revolution and advise government on how Uganda should adopt them.

I joined from the Ministry of ICT's Government Citizen Interaction Centre, a few months after finishing university, and met the President with the rest of the team when he launched it.

Over the next eighteen months we studied how other countries were preparing and wrote the report that became Uganda's national 4IR strategy: skills, infrastructure, research, cyber security and data protection, aimed at making Uganda a 4IR hub by 2040. The draft went public in October 2020, and the final report was handed to the Prime Minister in December 2022.

Links: [Read the appointment on the Ministry of ICT site](https://dmu.ict.go.ug/he-museveni-appoints-4th-industrial-revolution-taskforce)

Photo caption: President Museveni talks to Akbr Kanyesigye at the launch, as ICT Minister Frank Tumwebaze looks on. April 2019. Photo: Ministry of ICT and National Guidance.

### Kyankwanzi, 2026

Political Education, Transformative and Leadership Development Course. National Leadership Institute, Kyankwanzi. Completed 30 July 2026.

A residential course about loving and serving your country. The lectures ran through Uganda's history from before colonial rule, political economy, how the country's position shapes its national goals, and what patriotism asks of a public servant. We sang in Kiswahili, marched in formation, and learned to think of the nation first.

The other half was military. Early mornings of drill and physical training, and time on the range learning to handle and shoot a rifle.

My syndicate's closing paper examined the impact of digital media and artificial intelligence on governance, national security, public opinion and socio-economic development in Uganda. It weighed online services and census tablets against deepfakes, cybercrime and the 2024 breach at the Bank of Uganda.

Along the way I built my classmates a small offline revision site, with flashcards, mock exams, a Kiswahili songbook and a shared leaderboard.

Links: [See the paper](https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/#pp-nali), [See it under education](https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/#ed-nali)

Photo caption: UBOS staff at the National Leadership Institute, Kyankwanzi, July 2026. Courtesy photo, via [New Vision](https://www.newvision.co.ug/category/news/ubos-staff-learn-swahili-self-defence-and-lea-NV_237811_072026).

### UBOS Innovation Award

Uganda Bureau of Statistics, 2025

The Bureau's innovation award for 2025. It recognised the work on the dissemination portal, which put the 2024 Census results online down to parish level, and on Sanyu, the AI assistant that answers from those figures and cites every one.

Links: [About Sanyu](https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/#p-sanyu), [About the portal](https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/#p-portal)

### Employee of the year

Uganda Bureau of Statistics, 2024

Ranked the best-performing staff member on the Bureau's appraisal for the 2024 National Population and Housing Census. That year I worked on the census from the first application to the last table.

- **Recruitment.** I was the primary developer of the e-recruitment and field staff system, which managed more than 200,000 census personnel.
- **Maps.** I wrote Python and QGIS scripts that sped up map preparation for the GIS team.
- **Enumeration.** I worked on the data collection tool the enumerators used on their tablets, restructured it so it ran faster, and helped cut the time it took to start enumeration.
- **Processing.** I automated steps of data processing in Python and helped bring AI into the coding of responses, which saved months of manual work.
Links: [About the census system](https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/#p-census), [The full role](https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/#xp-ubos)

### AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner

Amazon Web Services. Issued September 2025, valid until September 2028.

AWS describes it this way: earners have a fundamental understanding of IT services and their uses in the AWS Cloud, have demonstrated cloud fluency and foundational AWS knowledge, and can identify the essential AWS services needed to set up AWS-focused projects.

It sits behind the day job: I architect and run the Bureau's AWS and GCP estate, from Docker deployments to the shared outbound proxy.

Links: [Verify it on Credly](https://www.credly.com/badges/e7259f2c-476b-438c-b92f-f4642edbecc7)

### Huduma Fellow, class of 2026

LéO Africa Institute and Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung

Huduma is Swahili for service. The fellowship is a leadership programme for people who serve in Uganda's public and civic sectors, and each class takes in 15 fellows.

Fellows meet for seminars and workshops on leadership, public affairs and policy making, and go back to their workplaces in between, with mentorship, study tours and a project along the way. I joined the 2026 class from the Uganda Bureau of Statistics.

**Akbr Kanyesigye**IT Officer, Uganda Bureau of StatisticsAs listed among the Huduma Fellows

Links: [See the fellows](https://leoafricainstitute.org/programs/huduma-fellowship)

## Notes

### A wedding website for Conrad and Vanessa

23 September 2026. https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/notes/2026-09-a-wedding-website-for-conrad-and-vanessa.html

Conrad and Vanessa married on Friday 11 September 2026 at St George's Cathedral in Cape Town, with the reception that afternoon at Belair Pavilion in Paarl. Most of the people who love them live in Kampala, more than four thousand kilometres and one visa away. That distance shaped almost everything I built for them.

The site lives at [conradxvanessa.com](https://conradxvanessa.com). It started as a pledge form and grew, one section at a time, into the place where guests pledged, said whether they were coming, asked for help with a visa, chose a hotel and received their invitation card. Behind it sits a small back office that the wedding committee used every day.

*Screenshot: The home page, in the couple's navy and rose gold, counting down to the day.*

### Pledges, the way Ugandan weddings are paid for

In Uganda a wedding is carried by a crowd. Friends and family meet, pledge what they can, and pay it off over the months before the day. Conrad and Vanessa launched theirs at a wedding meeting in Kampala on 15 May 2026, and most guests first reached the site by scanning a QR code handed out that evening.

The pledge form asks for a name, a phone number, an amount in shillings and a reminder date, with quick buttons for fifteen days, the end of the month or thirty days. A thank-you goes out on WhatsApp straight away. It falls back to SMS for Ugandan numbers that WhatsApp can't reach, and goes by email too when the guest gives one. On the reminder date, an SMS goes out on its own. The page also lists the Mobile Money codes to pay with and three committee members to call.

*Screenshot: The pledge form, and the card every guest gets once they pledge.*

Every pledge comes with its own card, made from the guest's name and amount, in three photo designs and a tall one sized for a WhatsApp or Instagram story. A pledge card on someone's status is a public thank-you, and a quiet invitation to the next person.

### Getting Kampala to Cape Town

A wedding abroad means a visa for most Ugandan guests. The RSVP form asks the usual things: how many are coming, yes or love from afar, a note for the couple and a preferred hotel. One switch opens the rest: passport, work, who is paying for the trip, travel dates and any earlier South African visas, plus a choice of three group trips to the visa centre in June and July. Guests could change their answers through a personal link until 4 September.

Each guest still applied for their own visa. What the site does is gather what the couple's team needs to write every invitation letter, and give the committee a table it can filter and export for the visa office. A visa help page walks through the process, the cost and the dates, with the forms to download and a checklist.

*Screenshot: Guests who asked for visa help, as the committee saw them. It exports to a spreadsheet for the visa office.*

For the trip itself there are pages on the venue, flights, and six Cape Town hotels picked for the guests, filtered by budget with prices in both rand and shillings. Another page lists things to do across the five days of celebrations, from 9 to 13 September.

### Invitations, one guest at a time

The invitation cards come in four designs, from light and floral to deep burgundy. Each carries the guest's name in script, the order of the day, and a QR code back to the RSVP page. The committee issues them from the back office, one guest at a time or straight from a pledge, and downloads them as images or PDFs sized for a 5 by 7 inch print or A4, or as one ZIP file for a whole batch.

*Screenshot: Two of the four designs, printed for made-up guests.*

*Screenshot: The card maker. Pick a design, type a name, download.*

### The committee's side

Most of the work happened in the back office. The pledges page shows what was pledged, what was collected and what is still owed. From there the committee can search, filter, record part payments, and send reminders in bulk by SMS, WhatsApp or email. Every message the site sends lands in one log, so nobody has to wonder whether a guest heard from us.

My favourite part is the smallest. The committee already kept its pledge list in a WhatsApp group, with an emoji beside each name for paid or pending. Rather than ask anyone to retype it, the back office takes the pasted list, reads the emoji, converts pledges made in dollars, and brings them all in.

*Screenshot: Pledges in the back office, with made-up guests: the totals first, then every pledge with its payment state and reminder date.*

Access is by role. Admins run everything, editors keep the records up to date, and viewers can look without changing anything.

### Built for the phone in your hand

Nearly every guest arrived from a phone, usually from a QR code or a link in a WhatsApp group, so every page was designed at phone width first.

*Screenshot: The home page and the RSVP form on a phone.*

Under the hood it is plain: HTML, CSS and a little JavaScript, with no framework. It began on Cloudflare Pages, with Pages Functions for the API, a D1 database, and Workers KV for admin sign-ins. Later it moved to a small server of its own, where a thin Node wrapper runs the same functions unchanged against SQLite, behind nginx. WhatsApp messages go out through a command-line tool on that server, SMS through EgoSMS, and email through Resend.

The site grew in the open. Sections went live as the wedding needed them, nine of twelve in the end, while the couple's story, the guide for the day and the guestbook stayed behind the scenes.

Congratulations, Conrad and Vanessa. May the marriage outlast the website by a very long time.

Every screenshot here uses made-up guests, phone numbers and passports. No real guest's details appear in this post.

### Five rules for AI over official statistics

4 August 2026. https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/notes/2026-08-five-rules-for-ai-over-official-statistics.html

Generative systems are arriving in statistical dissemination across the continent this year, often procured quickly and judged more on how fluent they sound than on whether the numbers are right. A model that produces a confident, wrong district population hands the reputational bill to the office that published it. Official statistics carry value only because the public accepts the figure.

So before Sanyu goes out as a public service of the Bureau, we wrote down the conditions we had to meet to feel safe releasing it. Five clauses, each one drawn from something the build itself forced on us. They're short enough to check.

### 1. Figures originate in the statistical system

The model selects what to retrieve; the database supplies the value. A number reaches the user only when a structured query returned it. This is the whole architecture in one sentence. The language model never generates a figure, it emits a typed function call, and the verified result is placed into the answer verbatim.

### 2. Every figure carries its source

Source table, survey or census, reference period and geography travel with the value, in a form the user can follow back to the publication. Charts render from the same verified values as the surrounding text, so a picture can't disagree with its caption.

### 3. The system declines outside its data

Where a question falls beyond published statistics, the correct response says so plainly. Silence about a limit counts as a defect. This one was harder to build than it sounds, because a fluent model would much rather answer.

### 4. Evaluation is published before launch

A named benchmark with ground truth, plus a regression suite that asserts exact published figures, runs automatically on every build. Ours has 45 deterministic tests, including a set of golden facts that must match the printed census tables to the digit. The results are public.

### 5. A statistician signs

Generated narrative passes a named human reviewer before publication. The machine drafts; the office remains the author.

> The code demonstrates that the conditions are achievable, because the system standing beside it meets them.

None of these rules is about a particular vendor or model. They're conditions any statistics office could adopt this year, and we'd like other offices to argue with them, adapt them, and tell us what we missed. The technical details of how Sanyu meets them are on the [work page](https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/#p-sanyu).

### A week in Rome with SDMX

6 October 2025. https://kanyeceejaya.github.io/notes/2025-10-a-week-in-rome-with-sdmx.html

Ivan Atwiine and I spent last week at the 10th SDMX Global Conference in Rome, hosted by the Bank of Italy. Three days of plenaries, then two days of training. The theme was "Smarter data for better insights", and the invitation had asked for exactly the kind of work we do: AI and machine learning applied to statistical pipelines, and dissemination tools that people actually use.

We went to talk about the pipeline. The paper, "From fragmentation to intelligence", describes how UBOS pulls administrative, survey and census data straight from source systems into one platform, validates it on the way in, and publishes it through the national dashboard. The rule-based checks catch the obvious; the machine learning helps with anomalies, cleaning and classifying community-level submissions. It's the plumbing behind everything else the Bureau now does with data.

### What I took home

**SDMX is a join key, not a file format.** I had been treating it as a way to publish. The better way to see it: once two datasets share the same concepts, code lists and dimensions, a question that crosses them becomes cheap to answer. That is precisely what a chatbot over official statistics needs. Most of the effort in grounding a language model is agreeing on what an indicator means, and SDMX is that agreement, written down.

**Validation can be data too.** The sessions on SDMX 3.0 and VTL, the validation and transformation language, described rules as something you exchange rather than something buried in a script. We write ours in Python. Some of them should probably live next to the data instead.

**Everyone's problem is fragmentation.** Central banks, statistical offices, international agencies: the stories differed in scale, not in kind. The exciting demos all rested on the boring, careful part, which is people agreeing on structure. That was reassuring. It is the part we can control.

The two training days made the tooling concrete: data structure definitions, dataflows, registries. It's one thing to read the standard, another to build a dataflow with someone who has done it a hundred times and watch where they slow down.

### What changed back home

We came back and started a prototype: take survey tables from the demographic and health survey and the household survey, and turn them into SDMX-ready structures. Reusable structure definitions by table shape rather than one per table, and a crosswalk of indicators so we can say quickly whether a figure exists in one survey, the other, or both. It's the first step toward cross-dataset retrieval, chatbot queries that span surveys, and briefs that write themselves from verified numbers.

Rome itself: warm, loud, and exactly as good at coffee as advertised.
